title: Reliably reverse advanced atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment capability that makes advanced atherosclerosis extensively and durably reversible across the body’s arteries. It would resolve established plaques while restoring stable, functional arterial structure, including in arteries with advanced fibrotic and calcified disease. Safe repair would require preserving vessel integrity, avoiding plaque rupture and thrombosis, and controlling recurrence. These are proposed requirements for the breakthrough. The supplied evidence establishes a narrower foundation in coronary plaque treatment.

Existing lipid-lowering treatment provides a starting point. The FITTER report describes reductions in recurrent coronary events with statin treatment and summarizes evidence that lipid lowering can produce plaque regression and improve plaque composition over time. The proposed advance extends that foundation to extensive repair of advanced disease, with durable structural and functional benefits across multiple vascular territories.

significance.text: Conditional on successful development, extensive plaque resolution and stable arterial repair would make a widespread, cumulative disease substantially reversible. The direct achievement would be recovery of diseased arterial structure and function. The coronary rationale for pursuing this is substantial. FITTER explains that, after treatment of the culprit lesion in acute coronary syndrome, many recurrent myocardial infarctions arise from other pre-existing atherosclerotic lesions. Treating this residual disease could therefore have consequences beyond the initially treated site.

Conditional impact synthesis. Fewer myocardial infarctions, ischemic strokes and cardiovascular deaths are plausible downstream goals if repair safely reduces clinically important disease in the relevant arteries. Each benefit would require clinical demonstration. Plaque reversal would leave other causes of these events to be addressed, and an improvement in plaque imaging alone would leave the magnitude of clinical benefit unresolved. The supplied coronary trial provides no demonstrated whole-body repair, stroke-prevention or mortality benefit.

The extent of the achievement would depend on which lesions, patients and arterial territories respond, how much function is recovered, and how long the repair lasts. Several successfully treated territories could demonstrate broad applicability. A finite set of observations would still leave questions about efficacy in additional arterial beds and lesion types.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap. The central challenge is to achieve extensive, durable regression together with stable repair in people who already have advanced atherosclerosis. The engineering target includes fibrotic and calcified lesions, preservation of vessel integrity during treatment, avoidance of rupture, thrombosis and vessel injury, and sustained control of recurrence. The supplied evidence does not establish the technical feasibility of resolving each of these lesion components or the comprehensive availability of such treatment.

Scientific and engineering synthesis. A convincing intervention would need to coordinate removal or remodeling of diseased material with maintenance of a mechanically stable arterial wall. It would also need to produce beneficial structural change alongside preserved or improved physiological function. Addressing one plaque feature leaves the response of other components unresolved, so lipid depletion, fibrosis, calcification and vessel function would need separate assessment where relevant.

Proposed translational barriers include achieving consistent effects across different vascular territories and advanced lesion types, identifying patients who benefit, establishing a practical treatment regimen, and sustaining repair under continuing disease risk. FITTER contributes evidence about short-term coronary treatment and explicitly calls for longer follow-up and clinical-outcome assessment. Its scope leaves advanced fibrotic and calcified disease, whole-tree repair and long-term recurrence control incompletely documented.

current_state.text: Partial plaque regression is already possible. The FITTER authors summarize prior GLAGOV, PACMAN-AMI and HUYGENS findings as showing incremental plaque regression when PCSK9 inhibitors were added to high-intensity statin therapy. They also describe statin-associated reductions in recurrent events and improvements in plaque composition over time. These earlier trial findings are available here through FITTER’s account. Their underlying publications were outside the supplied review’s inspected materials.

The randomized, placebo-controlled FITTER trial, published on 18 August 2025, assigned 150 patients with acute coronary syndrome and relevant non-culprit coronary lesions to evolocumab or placebo added to high-intensity statin therapy. Over 12 weeks, neither primary endpoint showed a statistically significant between-group improvement. The reported p-values were 0.6 for fractional flow reserve and 0.8 for maximum lipid core burden index within a 4 mm segment.

Fractional flow reserve is a pressure-based measure of coronary lesion physiology. The maximum lipid core burden index within a 4 mm segment characterizes a localized plaque lipid feature. Together, these endpoints assess selected physiological and morphological aspects of coronary disease. They leave extensive structural repair across the arterial tree untested. The 12-week findings also leave longer treatment durations and other interventions open to investigation. FITTER’s authors explicitly call for longer follow-up and assessment of clinical outcomes.

The supplied review assessed the full, untruncated main article text, including methods and tabulated results. Linked supplements and figure images were outside its inspected materials. The text and tables supported the reported trial population, duration and primary comparisons. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results, so it cannot establish the comprehensive treatment landscape or whether the full proposed capability remained unavailable as of 1 November 2026. Its source retrieval date of 11 November 2026 adds no evidence about intervening developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Show extensive regression and stable arterial repair in people with advanced atherosclerosis across several prespecified vascular territories, with deliberate inclusion and characterization of fibrotic and calcified disease. Before testing, define the required magnitude of regression, the structural and functional measures of repair, the follow-up duration needed to demonstrate durability, and acceptable safety thresholds. These are proposed assessment requirements whose numerical values remain to be established.
completion_criteria.label: Extensive regression and stable arterial repair across prespecified vascular territories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical confirmation. Randomized trials against excellent contemporary care should demonstrate fewer clinically important cardiovascular events with acceptable safety. Prespecified analyses should establish which outcomes improve and in which populations, including myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke or mortality where those benefits are claimed. Longer follow-up should assess persistence of repair, recurrent plaque disease and delayed harms. FITTER supports the need for longer follow-up and clinical-outcome assessment, while the broader completion framework is a proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate fewer cardiovascular events with acceptable safety

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries. Independent teams should reproduce the principal structural, functional and clinical findings using transparent measurement methods. Studies should document the treatment burden, eligibility limits, maintenance requirements and performance across the tested lesion types and vascular territories. Any claim of broad applicability should state its demonstrated coverage and remaining gaps. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth, with further evidence needed for additional arterial beds and patient groups.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of principal findings with documented practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. CAR-12, Detect actionable coronary plaque risk before a first clinical event, overlaps most directly through identification of plaques and patients who could benefit from intervention. Its central capability is early risk detection and actionability. CAR-02 concerns reversal and repair of established advanced disease. Detection could support treatment selection and monitoring, while each concept retains its own completion requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-10, Reverse established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement, shares the ambition of reversing established cardiovascular pathology and may involve related questions about calcified tissue remodeling. CAR-10 targets aortic valve disease, while CAR-02 targets atherosclerotic disease in arterial walls. CAR-11, Reverse pulmonary arterial hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences, shares an interest in vascular repair and physiological recovery, with a distinct pulmonary vascular disease target.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-01, Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart, and CAR-08, Durably reverse heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, concern myocardial recovery and heart-failure physiology. Arterial repair could complement those goals where atherosclerotic disease contributes to cardiac injury or dysfunction. Each would still require direct evidence for recovery of its target condition.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-03, A durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart, CAR-04, A dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts, and CAR-07, Produce a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart, address replacement of severely diseased hearts. Their overlap with CAR-02 lies in reducing the consequences of cardiovascular disease. Their completion depends on replacement-heart performance, availability and durability, whereas CAR-02 requires repair of the patient’s arterial disease. Systemic arterial health could remain relevant after heart replacement.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-05, Correct inherited heart disease directly and durably in the beating heart, shares the goal of durable disease modification, with an inherited cardiac target. CAR-06, Make most preventable sudden cardiac deaths predictable and preventable, and CAR-09, A durable, non-ablative cure for atrial fibrillation, address prediction and prevention of sudden death and treatment of an arrhythmia, respectively. Successful arterial repair could affect some ischemia-related risks, while those concepts encompass additional mechanisms and require their own demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-13, Broadly prevent cardiac injury from cancer treatment without weakening cancer control, overlaps through cardiovascular injury prevention and preservation of cardiac health. Its defining requirement includes protection during cancer treatment while maintaining cancer control. CAR-02 instead targets established advanced atherosclerotic disease across the arterial tree.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence cannot establish whether extensive, durable repair of advanced atherosclerosis across the arterial tree remained unavailable as of 1 November 2026.
The technical basis and feasibility of safely resolving advanced fibrotic and calcified arterial lesions require evidence beyond the supplied coronary trial.
Numerical thresholds for extensive regression, stable repair, durability and acceptable safety remain unspecified.
The vascular territories, lesion types and patient populations needed to substantiate broad applicability remain to be defined.
The magnitude of any benefit for myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, mortality and long-term recurrence remains undemonstrated for the proposed capability.
Linked FITTER supplements, figure images and the original publications of the prior regression trials were outside the supplied review’s inspected materials.

brief.title: Lasting repair of diseased arteries throughout the body
possible: People with advanced artery disease could have plaques, the deposits that build up in artery walls, extensively cleared or reshaped throughout the body. Treatment would restore stable, working arteries, including those with scar-like tissue and hardened calcium deposits.
The repair would last, with treatment controlling the return of plaques while preserving artery walls and avoiding plaque rupture and blood clots.
why: For people with advanced disease, this would mean recovering artery structure and function after years of accumulating damage.

Repair across the body could reduce heart attacks, strokes caused by blocked blood flow, and cardiovascular deaths. Treating disease beyond an initially treated blockage matters because many repeat heart attacks arise from other existing plaques.

sources.showed: The FITTER trial tested evolocumab, a cholesterol-lowering drug, added to intensive statin treatment. After 12 weeks, it found no statistically significant added improvement in pressure-based blood-flow measurements or plaque fat content in heart arteries.
sources.quote: No between-group differences in any IVUS-derived parameter were found.
sources.cited_for: Partial plaque regression is possible, but this short trial found no added improvement on its main measures.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish lasting repair of advanced plaques throughout the body or fewer cardiovascular events from such repair.

sources.showed: In a selected group of 33 people, cholesterol-lowering treatment reduced plaque fat in the carotid arteries in the neck. Imaging also showed a reduction in the proportion of the artery occupied by its wall in fat-rich regions.
sources.quote: Intensive lipid therapy significantly depletes carotid plaque lipid.
sources.cited_for: Cholesterol-lowering treatment can reduce plaque fat and produce partial regression in neck arteries.
sources.not_established: This small analysis did not establish extensive repair of advanced scarred or calcified plaques across the body's arteries.

shown: Partial plaque shrinkage is already possible with cholesterol-lowering treatment. Xue-Qiao Zhao and colleagues used magnetic resonance imaging, which produces detailed internal images, to track reduced plaque fat and partial regression in neck arteries in a selected group of 33 people.

Frans B Mensink and colleagues tested additional cholesterol lowering in people with significant heart-artery disease. FITTER found no statistically significant added benefit on its main blood-flow and plaque-fat measures over 12 weeks.
missing: No treatment has demonstrated extensive, lasting repair of advanced plaques across several artery regions, including scarred and calcified disease.
Repair must preserve artery strength and function without causing plaque rupture, blood clots or vessel injury.
Trials must establish whether this repair reduces major cardiovascular events and keeps disease from returning over the long term.

milestones.label: Extensive, stable repair across several artery regions
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to show extensive, lasting plaque reduction and stable artery structure and function across predefined regions, including scarred and calcified disease. This would establish broad repair of advanced disease.

milestones.label: Fewer cardiovascular events with acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show fewer major cardiovascular events than excellent current care, with acceptable safety and lasting benefits. This would establish that repair improves health beyond changes on scans.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation and clear treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce structural, functional and clinical benefits using transparent measures and document eligibility, treatment burden, maintenance and coverage. This would establish reliability and practical limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether advanced scarred and calcified plaques can be safely resolved while maintaining a strong, functional artery wall.
The required amount of plaque reduction, duration of repair and acceptable safety thresholds remain undefined.
Which artery regions, plaque types and patient groups would establish broad applicability remains unresolved.

page.title: Reversal of advanced systemic atherosclerosis
page.definition: Treatment reverses established plaques across affected arterial territories, including plaques dominated by fibrous tissue or calcium deposits. The artery walls recover normal structure and function, the repair persists, and patients have fewer cardiovascular events. For comparison, adding evolocumab to statin therapy reduced the share of an imaged coronary artery segment occupied by plaque by about one percentage point in GLAGOV.

goal.need: After an acute coronary syndrome, patients can remain at high risk despite intensive statin therapy. Among placebo recipients with persistent abnormal blood lipids, 10.0% with one affected arterial territory, 22.2% with two and 39.7% with three died of coronary disease, had a heart attack or ischaemic stroke, or were hospitalised for unstable angina over a median 2.8 years. Statins can reduce fatty plaque while dense calcium increases. The value of repairing advanced plaques would be preventing further events beyond those already prevented by lipid lowering.

figures.caption: FOURIER participants experiencing the primary cardiovascular endpoint
figures.note: The composite comprised cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalisation for unstable angina or coronary revascularisation. These are reported event proportions, not annual rates.

statements.body: The Lancet Commission on rethinking coronary artery disease
statements.quote: We recommend that all guidelines emphasise that prevention, reversal, or cure should be the aim of the treatment of atherosclerosis.

statements.body: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
statements.quote: Severe atherosclerosis may not be fully reversible with currently available treatments.

completion.title: Advanced systemic atherosclerosis reverses with maintained arterial repair and clinical benefit.
completion.criterion: Randomized human evidence demonstrates that the treatment restores normal arterial structure and function across affected territories in advanced atherosclerosis, including fibrotic and calcified plaques. Follow-up demonstrates sustained restoration and superiority to contemporary care on a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction or non-fatal stroke. A blinded, independent committee adjudicates events. The benefit–risk assessment includes plaque rupture, thrombosis and vessel injury.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of NHLBI’s restoration description, the Lancet Commission’s reversal goal and EMA’s clinical outcome guidance. No external body was identified that defines the combined test.
completion.basis: EMA defines a preferred clinical endpoint for lipid-disorder trials. It allows linked imaging and outcome evidence from an embedded study or from independent studies with comparable populations and concordant effects of the intervention. Numerical cutoffs for normal arterial structure and function, the duration of maintained repair and an acceptable excess of vascular harm remain undefined for systemic reversal.

milestones.title: An animal experiment shows established arterial plaque shrinking below pretreatment burden at p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Compare histological lesion area at the same arterial site in treated animals and in a reference group examined when treatment begins. Mean lesion area after treatment must be below the pretreatment mean at two-sided p<0.05 under the published analysis. In the mouse protocol, lesions are established during six months on an atherogenic diet and assessed 12 weeks after treatment begins.
milestones.set_by: Van Craeyveld and colleagues, published experimental protocol, 2011; the test was applied to mouse aortic-root and brachiocephalic lesions, not established as a regulatory preclinical requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: A two-sided p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

milestones.title: MRI shows less lipid in human carotid plaques at three years than at baseline.
milestones.criterion: In participants with a measurable lipid-rich necrotic core on baseline carotid MRI, compare core volume in matched plaque regions at baseline and year three. Test whether the mean within-participant change is below zero. The CPC protocol uses contrast-enhanced MRI at baseline and at years one, two and three to establish the time course.
milestones.set_by: Carotid Plaque Composition study, NCT00715273, study protocol and statistical analysis plan.
milestones.threshold_quote: To test the primary hypothesis that intensive lipid therapy decreases carotid plaque lipid content assessed by CE-MRI.

milestones.title: Plaque volume regresses more than control treatment in a randomized human trial at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized trial with paired imaging of the same arterial segment, plaque volume must fall below baseline in the treatment group and the change must favour treatment over control at two-sided p<0.05. GLAGOV’s primary measure is the change from baseline to week 78 in percent atheroma volume, the proportion of the imaged coronary vessel occupied by plaque. Normalized total atheroma volume is a prespecified secondary measure.
milestones.set_by: GLAGOV investigators, registered trial NCT01813422 and published analysis; the volume definition and imaging schedule were written for coronary arteries.
milestones.threshold_quote: Regression was defined as any decrease in PAV or TAV from baseline.

milestones.title: Human plaque burden regresses in two vascular beds assessed by two different imaging techniques.
milestones.criterion: For the same treatment, demonstrate a decrease from baseline in plaque burden in each of two arterial territories assessed by two different imaging techniques. Document the validity and reliability of each technique at the site where it is used. EMA describes this combination as stronger evidence for estimating overall burden.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, CHMP Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in the treatment of lipid disorders, revision 3, section 4.1.3; a recommendation for assessing systemic burden.
milestones.threshold_quote: In this context, data generated from two different vascular beds by two different techniques is considered more robust in estimating the overall atherosclerotic burden.

milestones.title: Treatment restores normal arterial structure and function in advanced human atherosclerotic plaques.
milestones.criterion: In a prospective controlled human study, document advanced fibrotic and calcified plaques before treatment. Demonstrate regression of these plaques and recovery of both normal arterial wall structure and physiological function across the affected territories. Assess structure and function separately in the territories for which restoration is claimed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis of NHLBI’s description of recovery and the Lancet Commission’s reversal goal. No external numerical standard for restoration of advanced plaques was identified.

milestones.title: Plaque regression on imaging is linked to fewer cardiovascular events with the same treatment.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the relationship between the treatment’s effect on the plaque imaging measure and its effect on clinically relevant cardiovascular events in the intended patient population. EMA permits an adequately sized study with early imaging and longer clinical follow-up. Its preferred design uses independent studies with comparable baseline populations and treatment effects in the same direction.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, CHMP guideline on lipid disorders, revision 3, section 4.1.3, for an indication based on vascular imaging.
milestones.threshold_quote: the necessary link between the marker, clinical event and the influence of the therapeutic intervention on imaging measures

not_found: No published criterion was found defining durable reversal of advanced fibrotic and calcified atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree.
No external cutoff was found for restored arterial structure and function, required territorial coverage, durability or acceptable excess vascular harm.
No human trial was identified showing sustained structural and functional recovery across advanced fibrotic and calcified arterial territories together with fewer major cardiovascular events.

results.finding: Carotid MRI in 61 participants receiving atorvastatin plus niacin showed a mean annualized lipid-rich necrotic core volume change of −15.1 mm³/year.
In acute coronary syndrome patients treated with atorvastatin (n=24), coronary plaque volume decreased 13.1% from baseline at 6 months.
results.detail: Of 70 randomized patients, 48 had paired intravascular ultrasound measurements. Coronary angiography was performed during emergency care, and the reported plaque-volume change came from ultrasound alone.
results.quote: Plaque volume was significantly reduced in the atorvastatin group (13.1+/-12.8% decrease) compared with the control group (8.7+/-14.9% increase; P<0.0001).

results.finding: Among 86 patients with acute coronary syndrome after PCI, coronary plaque regression or stability on ultrasound was associated with fewer major events (adjusted HR 0.26).
results.detail: The cohort had 13 events. Early atorvastatin use was more common in the regression group, and subsequent statin type and dose varied.
results.quote:
Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for plaque 
regression, age, gender, BMI, hypertension, diabetes 
and type of ACS revealed that plaque regression was 
significantly predictive for MACCE (HR, 0.26; 95% 
CI, 0.07 to 0.83; p  ̞0.023; Table 4).

results.finding: In 180 patients with acute coronary syndrome after emergency PCI, early atorvastatin was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.46 for a first major cardiac or cerebrovascular event.
results.detail: The follow-up study reports the clinical outcome and cites the earlier imaging result without reporting an analysis linking them.
results.quote: Furthermore, by adjusting for validated prognosticators, early statin administration was identified as a good predictor of MACCE (HR 0.46, 95%CI 0.23-0.86; p=0.015).

results.finding: In FOURIER (n=27,564), evolocumab added to statins reduced the primary cardiovascular composite versus placebo (HR 0.85).
results.quote:
Relative to placebo, evolocumab treatment significantly reduced the risk of the primary 
end point (1344 patients [9.8%] vs. 1563 patients [11.3%]; hazard ratio, 0.85; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.92; P<0.001)

results.finding: In 18,924 patients with recent acute coronary syndrome, alirocumab reduced the risk of the primary cardiovascular composite versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.85).
results.quote:
A composite primary end-point event oc-
curred in 903 patients (9.5%) in the alirocumab group and in 1052 patients (11.1%) in the 
placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.78 to 0.93; P<0.001).

results.finding: In 1,007 SPARCL participants with baseline carotid stenosis, atorvastatin reduced the hazard of any stroke by 33%.
results.quote: In the group with carotid artery stenosis, treatment with atorvastatin was associated with a 33% reduction in the risk of any stroke (hazard ratio [HR] 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47, 0.94; P=0.02), and a 43% reduction in risk of major coronary events (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.32, 1.00; P=0.05).

definition = "Treatment reverses established plaques across affected arterial territories, including plaques dominated by fibrous tissue or calcium deposits. The artery walls recover normal structure and function, the repair persists, and patients have fewer cardiovascular events. For comparison, adding evolocumab to statin therapy reduced the share of an imaged coronary artery segment occupied by plaque by about one percentage point in GLAGOV.". Reason: A measured example of partial coronary regression makes the scale of the proposed restoration clear.

goal.need = "After an acute coronary syndrome, patients can remain at high risk despite intensive statin therapy. Among placebo recipients with persistent abnormal blood lipids, 10.0% with one affected arterial territory, 22.2% with two and 39.7% with three died of coronary disease, had a heart attack or ischaemic stroke, or were hospitalised for unstable angina over a median 2.8 years. Statins can reduce fatty plaque while dense calcium increases. The value of repairing advanced plaques would be preventing further events beyond those already prevented by lipid lowering.". Reason: The current text gives trial enrolment as its measure of scale and omits both the risk associated with disease in several territories and the limits of plaque shrinkage as evidence of benefit.

edit completion: criterion = "Randomized human evidence demonstrates that the treatment restores normal arterial structure and function across affected territories in advanced atherosclerosis, including fibrotic and calcified plaques. Follow-up demonstrates sustained restoration and superiority to contemporary care on a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction or non-fatal stroke. A blinded, independent committee adjudicates events. The benefit\u2013risk assessment includes plaque rupture, thrombosis and vessel injury."; set_by = "Atlas synthesis of NHLBI\u2019s restoration description, the Lancet Commission\u2019s reversal goal and EMA\u2019s clinical outcome guidance. No external body was identified that defines the combined test."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; basis = "EMA defines a preferred clinical endpoint for lipid-disorder trials. It allows linked imaging and outcome evidence from an embedded study or from independent studies with comparable populations and concordant effects of the intervention. Numerical cutoffs for normal arterial structure and function, the duration of maintained repair and an acceptable excess of vascular harm remain undefined for systemic reversal."; refs = [2, 4, 5]. Reason: The current wording leaves it unclear whether superiority applies to a composite or to each component and omits EMA’s independent blinded adjudication.
add case "Thoracic aorta". Reason: A randomized human trial measured thoracic aortic plaques and demonstrated a response distinct from that of abdominal aortic plaques.
add case "Abdominal aorta". Reason: The abdominal aorta was assessed separately in the same trial, where atorvastatin at 20 mg slowed progression without producing regression.

edit m1: criterion = "Compare histological lesion area at the same arterial site in treated animals and in a reference group examined when treatment begins. Mean lesion area after treatment must be below the pretreatment mean at two-sided p<0.05 under the published analysis. In the mouse protocol, lesions are established during six months on an atherogenic diet and assessed 12 weeks after treatment begins."; threshold_quote = "A two-sided p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 14, 15]. Reason: The mouse group sizes and observed reductions obscure the essential comparison with plaque burden before treatment.

edit m2: title = "MRI shows less lipid in human carotid plaques at three years than at baseline."; criterion = "In participants with a measurable lipid-rich necrotic core on baseline carotid MRI, compare core volume in matched plaque regions at baseline and year three. Test whether the mean within-participant change is below zero. The CPC protocol uses contrast-enhanced MRI at baseline and at years one, two and three to establish the time course."; set_by = "Carotid Plaque Composition study, NCT00715273, study protocol and statistical analysis plan."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "To test the primary hypothesis that intensive lipid therapy decreases carotid plaque lipid content assessed by CE-MRI."; threshold_ref = 16; refs = [7, 16]. Reason: The registered carotid protocol specifies the site, imaging method and direction of change, while the present criterion also reports participant counts and outcomes.

edit m3: criterion = "In a randomized trial with paired imaging of the same arterial segment, plaque volume must fall below baseline in the treatment group and the change must favour treatment over control at two-sided p<0.05. GLAGOV\u2019s primary measure is the change from baseline to week 78 in percent atheroma volume, the proportion of the imaged coronary vessel occupied by plaque. Normalized total atheroma volume is a prespecified secondary measure."; threshold_quote = "Regression was defined as any decrease in PAV or TAV from baseline."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 10, 17, 18]. Reason: The criterion needs both shrinkage below baseline and a randomized between-group difference, whereas the FITTER flow and lipid results measure other endpoints.

edit m4: criterion = "For the same treatment, demonstrate a decrease from baseline in plaque burden in each of two arterial territories assessed by two different imaging techniques. Document the validity and reliability of each technique at the site where it is used. EMA describes this combination as stronger evidence for estimating overall burden."; refs = [5]. Reason: The criterion currently mixes EMA’s multiterritory imaging recommendation with findings from two different treatments.

add milestone after m4: "Plaque regression on imaging is linked to fewer cardiovascular events with the same treatment.". Reason: The existing milestones cover structural and functional effects but omit EMA’s test for linking an imaging response to patient outcomes.

edit m5: criterion = "In a prospective controlled human study, document advanced fibrotic and calcified plaques before treatment. Demonstrate regression of these plaques and recovery of both normal arterial wall structure and physiological function across the affected territories. Assess structure and function separately in the territories for which restoration is claimed."; set_by = "Atlas synthesis of NHLBI\u2019s description of recovery and the Lancet Commission\u2019s reversal goal. No external numerical standard for restoration of advanced plaques was identified."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; refs = [2, 4, 5]. Reason: The final structural milestone needs a test of both wall recovery and physiological function, with the search verdict kept outside the criterion.

remove not found 2. Reason: West and colleagues found no significant femoral plaque regression in either randomized group, and Brunner and colleagues found no significant between-group difference in 24-month femoral wall-volume change.

add not found: "No human trial was identified showing sustained structural and functional recovery across advanced fibrotic and calcified arterial territories together with fewer major cardiovascular events.". Reason: The existing gaps concern the absence of an external criterion, while the distinct question of whether a published treatment meets the combined test is unresolved.
remove statement 1. Reason: The ACC page is Melvyn Rubenfire’s summary of a JACC review, so attributing its description of plaque regression to the College as an institutional goal is misleading.
